findings.title: GET /pulls/:id no longer refreshes from GitHub; stale data served silently
findings.rationale: The old handler attempted a live GitHub fetch and fell back to persisted data on failure. The new handler always returns persisted data without any GitHub call. Existing callers (e.g., CI scripts, other services) that depend on GET returning fresh data will now receive stale data until they explicitly call POST /pulls/:id/refresh. The response shape is identical, so no immediate breakage, but the behavioral change is silent and could cause incorrect downstream decisions (e.g., running a review on outdated diff).

findings.title: POST /pulls/:id/refresh lacks graceful fallback on GitHub failure
findings.rationale: The new POST endpoint throws an error if the GitHub API call fails. The old GET handler had a try-catch that served persisted data with a warning log. While an explicit refresh endpoint is expected to fail loudly, a fallback that returns the current persisted data (with a warning header) would make the endpoint more resilient and consistent with the previous behavior.

matched_title: GET /pulls/:id no longer refreshes PR data from GitHub, breaking callers that depend on implicit refresh

findings.title: GET /pulls/:id no longer refreshes PR data from GitHub, breaking callers that depend on implicit refresh
findings.rationale: The GET handler previously attempted to fetch PR detail from GitHub, update the DB, and return fresh data. If GitHub failed, it fell back to DB data. The new implementation removes the GitHub call entirely and returns only stored DB data. Any caller that relied on GET /pulls/:id to implicitly refresh PR data (e.g., a CI runner that calls this endpoint before running a review, or an external consumer) will now receive stale data. This can lead to incorrect review results or missing information. The PR description acknowledges this change but does not provide a migration path for existing callers.

findings.title: GET /pulls/:id no longer populates PR metadata (body, additions, deletions, filesCount) from GitHub on access
findings.rationale: Previously, the GET handler updated the PR record with body, additions, deletions, and filesCount from GitHub. Now it returns the stored values from the DB, which may be null or zero if the PR has never been refreshed. New PRs that have not been explicitly refreshed will show empty body, 0 additions/deletions, etc. While the web client has a refresh button, the initial load will be empty, and external callers may get incomplete data.

findings.title: GET /pulls/:id removed warning log when GitHub fetch fails, reducing observability
findings.rationale: The old code logged a warning when the GitHub fetch failed (e.g., no token or offline). The new code removes this log entirely. Operators lose visibility into when data might be stale.

matched_title: Missing authentication/authorization on new POST /pulls/:id/refresh

findings.title: Missing authentication/authorization on new POST /pulls/:id/refresh
findings.rationale: The new POST /pulls/:id/refresh route performs a GitHub API call and writes to the database (deleting and re-inserting files/commits, updating the PR row). Unlike the GET route, which is a pure read, this POST route has side effects and triggers outbound network calls. The diff shows no authentication or authorization check (e.g., no workspace membership verification, no token validation) before the refresh logic runs. An unauthenticated attacker who can reach the server could repeatedly hit this endpoint, causing: (1) excessive GitHub API usage (potential rate-limit exhaustion or cost), (2) unnecessary DB writes, and (3) potential data corruption if the attacker can influence the PR id. The GET route previously had the same GitHub call, but it was gated behind a token check and was a read; the new POST route is a write path and must be protected. The compatible alternative is to add the same authentication/authorization middleware used by other write routes (e.g., verify the caller's workspace membership and that the PR belongs to that workspace) before performing the refresh.

findings.title: New refresh endpoint is missing workspace authorization — cross-tenant PR read/write
findings.rationale: The new POST /pulls/:id/refresh handler calls resolvePrAndRepo(req.params.id, workspaceId) but the workspaceId is not derived from the authenticated session or the URL — it is undefined or attacker-controlled. The GET handler previously derived workspaceId from the authenticated request (req.workspaceId or similar). With the new route, any authenticated user can pass any PR id and read/overwrite files, commits, and the body of a PR that belongs to another workspace. This is a cross-tenant data exposure and integrity violation.

findings.rationale: The old GET /pulls/:id returned a PrDetail object that included the GitHub detail fields (additions, deletions, files_count, body, etc.) merged with the persisted record. The new GET returns a hand-built object that only includes a subset of fields (id, number, title, author, branch, files_count, files, commits) and omits the GitHub detail fields (additions, deletions, body, etc.). The existing client hook usePullDetail (client/src/lib/hooks/core.ts:119) and the PrDetail type (client/src/lib/types) still expect the old shape. A deployed caller that renders the PR detail page will now receive a response missing fields it relies on (e.g., body, additions, deletions), causing undefined values or rendering errors. This is a breaking change to the contract for the existing GET endpoint.

findings.title: Shared contract types diverge between server and client for new refresh endpoint
findings.rationale: The new POST /pulls/:id/refresh returns `{ ...detail, id: pr.id }` where `detail` is the GitHub API response. This shape is not the same as the PrDetail type used by the client (which expects fields like files_count, additions, deletions, etc. — the GitHub detail payload uses snake_case fields like files_count, additions, deletions, but the client's PrDetail type may expect camelCase or a different structure). The client's useRefreshPull hook (client/src/lib/hooks/core.ts:119) types the response as PrDetail, but the server returns a raw GitHub detail object. This mismatch means the client will receive fields it doesn't expect and miss fields it does, and the two shared contract copies (server and client) now disagree on the refresh endpoint's response type.

findings.title: Refresh endpoint error handling swallows GitHub failures
findings.rationale: The new POST /pulls/:id/refresh calls `container.github()` and `gh.getPullRequest(...)` without a try/catch. If the GitHub API call fails (rate limit, network error, 404), the endpoint will throw an unhandled error, resulting in a 500 response. The old GET /pulls/:id had a try/catch that logged a warning and served persisted data on failure. The new endpoint should handle GitHub failures gracefully, either by returning a 502/503 with a clear error or by falling back to the persisted data.

findings.rationale: The new POST /pulls/:id/refresh route resolves the PR via resolvePrAndRepo(req.params.id, workspaceId) but workspaceId is not defined in the route handler — it's not passed in the route params or request. matched_title: New POST /pulls/:id/refresh returns a different shape than the client expects

findings.title: New POST /pulls/:id/refresh returns a different shape than the client expects
findings.rationale: The new POST /pulls/:id/refresh handler returns `{ ...detail, id: pr.id }` where `detail` is the raw GitHub API response (snake_case fields like `files_count`, `additions`, `deletions`, `body`). But the client's `useRefreshPull` hook calls `api.post<PrDetail>(...)` and expects the `PrDetail` contract type (camelCase `filesCount`, `additions`, `deletions`, `body`, plus `files` and `commits` arrays). The old GET /pulls/:id returned a `PrDetail`-shaped object. So the refresh flow will fail at runtime: the client will receive a response that doesn't match the `PrDetail` type, and the subsequent `invalidateQueries` will refetch the GET, which now returns the persisted (stale) data — the refresh appears to succeed but shows stale data. findings.title: Route registration order may shadow the new POST /pulls/:id/refresh
findings.rationale: The new POST /pulls/:id/refresh route is registered after the GET /pulls/:id route in the same file. Fastify matches routes by method and path in registration order. If a request comes in as POST /pulls/123/refresh, Fastify will first check the GET /pulls/:id route — but since the method is POST, it won't match. However, if the framework or a plugin (e.g., a body parser or a method-override) treats the method as part of the path, the GET route could shadow the POST. This is a real risk that needs explicit verification. If the POST route is shadowed, the refresh endpoint will 404, breaking the client's refresh flow.

matched_title: GET /pulls/:id no longer refreshes from GitHub – behavioral contract change

findings.title: GET /pulls/:id no longer refreshes from GitHub – behavioral contract change
findings.rationale: Previously, GET /pulls/:id attempted to fetch fresh data from GitHub on every call (with a fallback to persisted data on failure). Now it always returns the persisted data without any network call. Any external caller (CI, other services, or future clients) that relied on GET to also trigger a refresh will now receive stale data. The response shape is unchanged, but the semantics of the endpoint have changed: it is no longer a 'get latest' operation. The PR description frames this as intentional, but the change is not communicated via a deprecation header or query parameter grace period.

findings.title: Response shape now always flat – fixes prior inconsistency
findings.rationale: The old GET had two return paths: the success path spread the GitHub API response (which uses nested objects like head.sha, base.ref) while the fallback path returned flat fields (head_sha, base). The new code always returns the flat shape. This aligns with the shared PrDetail type and eliminates a source of bugs. Callers that parsed the raw JSON and relied on the GitHub shape (e.g., response.head.sha) will break, but typed clients already expected the flat shape. This is a net improvement.

findings.title: POST /pulls/:id/refresh lacks graceful fallback on GitHub failure
findings.rationale: The new refresh endpoint calls `gh.getPullRequest()` without a try-catch. If GitHub is unreachable, rate-limited, or the token is missing, the endpoint will throw a 500 error. The old GET handled this gracefully by logging a warning and serving stale data. External callers using POST should expect transient failures and implement retry logic. The web client's useMutation will surface the error, but the UX could be improved by showing a fallback message.

findings.title: GET /pulls/:id no longer performs implicit GitHub refresh
findings.rationale: The old GET handler (lines 203–288) always attempted a live GitHub fetch and persisted the result before returning. The new handler (lines 203–240) serves only what is already stored in the database, with no network call. Any caller that depended on the GET endpoint to return the latest data from GitHub (e.g., an external integration that polls this endpoint for updates) will now receive stale data until it explicitly calls POST /pulls/:id/refresh. The response schema is unchanged, so no caller breaks immediately, but the semantics have changed.

findings.title: PRs without prior refresh may return incomplete data
findings.rationale: The new GET handler reads additions, deletions, files_count, files, and commits directly from the database. For PRs that have never been refreshed (e.g., newly created PRs or PRs imported without a GitHub fetch), these fields may be null, zero, or empty. Previously, the GET handler would attempt to fetch from GitHub and populate them on first access. This could affect consumers that expect these fields to be populated immediately after PR creation.

matched_title: New refresh route is missing workspaceId scoping — cross-workspace write

findings.title: New refresh route is missing workspaceId scoping — cross-workspace write
findings.rationale: The new POST /pulls/:id/refresh route calls resolvePrAndRepo(req.params.id, workspaceId) but never verifies that the resolved repo belongs to the caller's workspace. The GET route applies the same workspaceId filter to the pullRequests query, so it is scoped; the refresh route is not. A caller with a valid token can therefore refresh (and overwrite the body, additions, deletions, filesCount, and file/commit rows of) a PR in another workspace by guessing its id. This is a cross-workspace authorization bypass.

matched_title: GET /pulls/:id no longer fetches fresh data from GitHub

findings.title: GET /pulls/:id no longer fetches fresh data from GitHub
findings.rationale: The old handler (lines 207–215 in the original) attempted a live GitHub fetch and fell back to persisted data. The new handler returns only what is already in the database, with no network call. Any caller that depended on the implicit refresh (e.g., CI runner polling for new commits, external consumer expecting up-to-date files) will now silently receive stale data until someone explicitly calls POST /pulls/:id/refresh.

matched_title: GET /pulls/:id response narrowed to stored subset

findings.title: GET /pulls/:id response narrowed to stored subset
findings.rationale: The old handler returned the full GitHub PR detail (including fields like `labels`, `milestone`, `mergeable`, `requested_reviewers`, etc.) when a GitHub token was configured. The new handler always returns only the fields stored in the database (as defined by the shared PrDetail type). Any caller that relied on the extra GitHub-specific fields will now receive `undefined` for those fields and may behave differently. While the web client uses the shared types and is unaffected, external consumers or untyped callers could break silently.

findings.title: POST /pulls/:id/refresh response shape inconsistent with GET
findings.rationale: The POST endpoint returns `{ ...detail, id: pr.id }` where `detail` is the full GitHub PR detail, which may include fields not present in the GET response. This inconsistency could confuse clients that expect the same shape from both endpoints. It also means the POST response may contain fields not defined in the shared PrDetail type.

findings.title: Client hook URL construction with null prId
findings.rationale: The `useRefreshPull` hook constructs the URL as `/pulls/${prId}/refresh`. If `prId` is null or undefined, the URL becomes `/pulls/null/refresh` or `/pulls/undefined/refresh`. While the button is disabled when `!prId`, this is a latent bug if the hook is used elsewhere without a guard.

matched_title: GET /pulls/:id no longer returns additions/deletions/files_count — breaks existing callers

findings.title: GET /pulls/:id no longer returns additions/deletions/files_count — breaks existing callers
findings.rationale: The old GET handler returned the full GitHub detail payload (including additions, deletions, files_count) after a live fetch. The new GET handler builds a hand-picked object that omits those three fields. Any existing caller — the Pull Requests list, the detail page, or an external consumer — that reads additions/deletions/files_count from the GET response now gets undefined. This is a silent behavior change for every caller that relied on those fields being present.

findings.title: POST /pulls/:id/refresh returns a different shape than GET /pulls/:id — contract disagreement
findings.rationale: The new refresh route returns `{ ...detail, id: pr.id }` where `detail` is the raw GitHub payload (snake_case fields like files_count, additions, deletions). The GET route returns a hand-built object with camelCase fields (files_count, additions, deletions omitted). Both are typed as PrDetail, but they serialize to different JSON. A client that refreshes and then reads the response will see a different contract than the one used for the initial load — e.g. `files_count` vs `filesCount`, and missing `additions`/`deletions` in the GET case. This is a silent contract break for any caller that treats the two endpoints as interchangeable.

findings.title: Refresh route deletes files/commits before re-inserting without a transaction — partial state on failure
findings.rationale: The refresh route deletes all prFiles and prCommits for the PR, then re-inserts them. If the GitHub fetch succeeds but the insert fails (e.g. a constraint violation or a network blip), the PR is left with zero files/commits. The old code had the same delete-then-insert pattern, but it was inside the GET handler where a failure was caught and the persisted data was served. Now a refresh failure leaves the PR in a partial state that the GET will serve. This is a data-integrity regression for the new explicit refresh flow.

findings.title: New refresh endpoint performs a state-changing POST without CSRF protection
findings.rationale: The new POST /pulls/:id/refresh route mutates server state (deletes and re-inserts files/commits, updates the PR body and stats) and is triggered by a simple client-side fetch. If the application relies on cookie-based session auth (common in Fastify apps), this endpoint is vulnerable to cross-site request forgery: an attacker can craft a page that submits a POST to this endpoint on behalf of an authenticated user, causing the user's PR to be refreshed with attacker-influenced data (or, if the attacker can control the GitHub token, potentially overwriting the stored body/stats). The PR description and diff do not show any CSRF token, SameSite cookie attribute, or origin/referer check on this route. The existing GET route is read-only and not affected, but the new POST is a state-changing action that should be protected. This is a WARNING because the impact depends on the auth mechanism and whether the endpoint is same-site; however, it is a real security regression introduced by this PR.

matched_title: New POST /pulls/:id/refresh route is not registered — the diff only rewrites the GET handler, so the client's refresh call will 404 and the GET no longer refreshes.

findings.title: New POST /pulls/:id/refresh route is not registered — the diff only rewrites the GET handler, so the client's refresh call will 404 and the GET no longer refreshes.
findings.rationale: The diff shows the GET /pulls/:id handler being rewritten to a pure read (no GitHub call, no DB write) and the refresh logic being moved into a new POST handler. However, the diff does not show a new route registration for POST /pulls/:id/refresh — it only shows the GET handler being modified and the refresh logic being moved. The client's useRefreshPull posts to /pulls/:id/refresh, but without an explicit app.post registration, that request will hit the GET route (which only accepts GET) and return 404 or 405. This breaks the new client flow and, more importantly, changes the GET contract: previously GET /pulls/:id performed a GitHub refresh and returned fresh data; now it returns stale persisted data with no way to refresh via GET. Any caller that relied on the old GET behavior (e.g., the previous client flow or an external consumer) now gets stale data with no compatible alternative. The fix is to register the POST route with a distinct path (e.g., /pulls/:id/refresh) and keep the GET response shape identical to the previous persisted-detail shape, or add the refresh as an optional query param on the GET. Without that, the change breaks the existing contract.

matched_title: GET /pulls/:id no longer returns GitHub-derived fields (additions, deletions, files_count, body)

findings.title: GET /pulls/:id no longer returns GitHub-derived fields (additions, deletions, files_count, body)
findings.rationale: The old GET handler always fetched from GitHub and returned a detail object that included additions, deletions, files_count, and body (backfilled from the detail fetch). The new GET returns only the persisted DB fields (id, number, title, files_count, files, commits, etc.) and drops additions, deletions, and body. Any caller that read those fields from GET /pulls/:id — e.g. the Pull Requests list that shows real size/files, or any client that displays the PR body — now gets undefined. The client was updated to call refresh, but the shared contract types (vendor/shared) were not updated, and the server's GET response is not validated against PrDetail, so a 422 may not fire but the data is missing. This is a silent behavior change for every existing caller.

matched_title: Refresh route deletes persisted data before a successful GitHub fetch, breaking offline/rate-limited PR detail

findings.title: Refresh route deletes persisted data before a successful GitHub fetch, breaking offline/rate-limited PR detail
findings.rationale: The new POST /pulls/:id/refresh deletes all prFiles and prCommits rows for the PR before calling GitHub. If the GitHub call throws (rate limit, network, offline — the exact scenario the old GET handled by serving persisted data), the delete has already committed, so the PR detail page is left permanently empty. The old code explicitly caught this and served the persisted files/commits. This is a regression that breaks the offline/rate-limited caller.

findings.title: Refresh route returns raw GitHub detail payload, not the PrDetail contract shape
findings.rationale: The refresh route returns `{ ...detail, id: pr.id }` where `detail` is the raw GitHub getPullRequest response. The client's useRefreshPull hook types the response as PrDetail and refetches the GET /pulls/:id query on success. The GET route returns a different shape (files/commits arrays, files_count, etc.). The client will receive fields it doesn't expect and miss fields it does, causing the detail page to render with undefined/empty data after a refresh. The old GET returned the same shape as the new GET, so this is a contract break.

findings.title: Client refresh hook doesn't URL-encode the PR id, breaking non-numeric ids
findings.rationale: The useRefreshPull hook posts to `/pulls/${prId}/refresh` with no encodeURIComponent. If prId is ever non-numeric (e.g. a slug or a string with special chars), the request will 404 or be misinterpreted. The existing usePullDetail hook uses the same pattern, but it's a pre-existing issue; this new code copies it. Since the PR id comes from the URL param, it's likely numeric, but the contract should be explicit.

findings.title: GET /pulls/:id no longer backfills additions/deletions/filesCount, so the Pull Requests list shows stale/zero stats
findings.rationale: The old GET route fetched the GitHub detail and backfilled additions/deletions/filesCount into the pullRequests row, so the Pull Requests list always showed real size/files. The new GET is a pure read and never backfills; the backfill only happens in the new POST /refresh. So any PR that was never explicitly refreshed (or whose refresh failed) will show stale or zero stats in the list. This is a behavior change for the list view.

findings.title: Refresh route has no error handling; GitHub failure propagates as 500 and client shows 'Refreshing…' forever
findings.rationale: The refresh route calls gh.getPullRequest with no try/catch. If GitHub is rate-limited or offline, the error propagates as a 500. The client's useRefreshPull has no onError handler, so the mutation stays in 'pending' state and the button shows 'Refreshing…' indefinitely. The old GET route caught this and served persisted data. This is a UX and correctness regression.

findings.title: GET /pulls/:id now returns empty files/commits for PRs that were never refreshed, with no fallback or error
findings.rationale: The new GET route reads files/commits directly from the DB with no fallback. For a PR that was created before this change (or whose refresh failed), the DB has no files/commits, so the detail page renders empty with no indication of why. The old code had a fallback to fetch from GitHub. This is a silent data-loss regression for existing PRs.

findings.title: Shared contract types (PrDetail) not updated for the new refresh response shape
findings.rationale: The refresh route returns a different shape than the GET route, but the shared PrDetail type (in vendor/shared) is not changed in this diff. The client's useRefreshPull types the response as PrDetail, so the type system will not catch the mismatch. This is a contract drift between the two copies (server and client) that must be kept in sync.
